source.title: How do Multimodal Foundation Models Encode Text and Speech? An Analysis of Cross-Lingual and Cross-Modal Representations
source.authors: Hyunji Lee; Danni Liu; Supriti Sinhamahapatra; Jan Niehues

record.file_problem: None; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually measures cross-modal and cross-lingual representational similarity with SVCCA, and reports how it changes across layers and input conditions; it does not test model scaling or performance.
record.gate_note: The study reports qualitative trends from figures but no numerical SVCCA values in the text. It uses random vectors of matching sizes as a no-similarity baseline. The study does not compare alternative similarity metrics.
record.test_reason: No version is tested. The study compares speech and text activations for the same sentences inside each of three jointly trained speech-text models (Seamless, SONAR, SALMONN) using SVCCA, across layers and 30 languages. It does not compare independently trained models, vary scale or capability, or study vision-language pairs. It does not use seeds, stitching or maps, or interpretable features, and it uses only one metric. In SONAR, and partly the others, the cross-modal alignment is a training objective, so it is induced rather than arising independently. This is a related construct: within-model modality and language gaps. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that cross-modal representations converge over layers except in the initial layers, and that length adaptation is crucial but helps mainly high-resource languages. Speech shows larger cross-lingual differences than text. Without explicit alignment training the modality gap exceeds the language gap, so the models do not form fully unified semantic representations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SVCCA on semantically equivalent speech and text activations across layers and languages. It does not test scale or capability. The paper does not report a direct reproduction of the original sources' method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model, layer, language resource level, modality, and length-adaptation mechanism. SALMONN's text cross-lingual trend has an initial-layer exception; low-resource languages benefit less from the tested length adaptations.

fits_no_version.finding: Within three jointly trained speech-text models, SVCCA similarity between speech and text of the same sentence rises over layers after an early dip, but stays incomplete. It is lower for low-resource languages. The modality gap exceeds the language gap unless the model is explicitly trained to align (SONAR).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within multimodal or multilingual models, representations of semantically equivalent inputs converge with depth but stay incomplete. Explicit alignment objectives and input resource level govern how close they get.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-lingual similarity within a model is higher for text than for speech. Fragmented tokenization inflates input-layer cross-lingual similarity (r=0.228).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cross-lingual alignment depends on modality and tokenizer coverage.

fits_no_version.finding: Length-adaptation components slightly reduce the modality gap for high- and medium-resource languages, but not for low-resource ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture choices for length adaptation affect within-model cross-modal alignment, mainly for well-resourced languages.

record.problems: The analysis uses only intrinsic SVCCA measures and does not test downstream performance or alternative similarity metrics. It relies on FLEURS, whose examples are based on Wikipedia and may not generalize to informal or spoken domains. Only three models are studied; language coverage differs for SONAR; SALMONN prompts are not varied. Most plotted results are described qualitatively without numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: None. The retained rows capture the separately described model, resource-level, adaptation, modality, and token-sharing findings; the paper does not give further numerical per-language SVCCA values in the text.

untested.parts: No independently trained models, no comparison of scale or capability.
Speech-text inside single jointly trained models rather than separate vision and language models; model quality is not varied.
No mapping, stitching or transfer between models.
Only SVCCA with one setting (90% variance); no metric variation; no cross-model convergence measured.
No cross-model alignment measured; the role of shared data or objectives in independent models is not isolated.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V6/V7 links are rejected. Every measurement compares a single model's own speech and text pathways, which were trained jointly (SONAR with an explicit alignment loss). That makes this a study of within-model modality gaps, not of convergence between independently trained models. The paper does not cite the original sources. Nearly all results are figure-only, with no numbers.

versions.untested_parts: Does not scale models or compare model sizes, capability, or independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, and data.
Analyzes speech and text, not vision and language representations of paired images and captions; does not vary model quality or performance.
No comparison across random initialization seeds or analysis of shared features/subspaces across same-architecture networks.
SVCCA measures representational similarity; the study does not test mapping, stitching, transfer, or interchangeability.
Does not analyze recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Shows differences by language resource level, language, and model condition, but does not vary the similarity metric or its settings, or test out-of-distribution inputs.

Reports incomplete cross-modal and cross-lingual alignment and contrasts models with different alignment training, but does not isolate shared training data or objectives as causal explanations, or test a common model of reality.

rows.operation_detail: Measured SVCCA similarity between semantically equivalent speech and text representations across encoder layers.

conditions.value: sampled encoder layers; input embeddings and after length adaptor also analyzed

rows.measure: Average cross-modal SVCCA similarity over languages and layers.
rows.baseline: SVCCA of random vectors of the same sizes; numerical value not stated.
rows.value: Figure only; text states similarity generally increases through layers, with a dip in the initial layers.
rows.note: Qualitative trend is described in the text; no numerical layer scores are given.
rows.check: Within-model speech-text similarity in Seamless across layers. Not independently trained models, and no scale or capability variation, so it does not bear on V1, V2 or V7.

rows.measure: Average cross-modal SVCCA similarity over languages and layers.

rows.baseline: Cross-lingual text and speech similarities; numerical values not stated.
rows.value: Figure only; for most languages, intra-lingual cross-modal similarity exceeds the other similarity types.
rows.note: Authors say SONAR was explicitly trained to bridge modality and language gaps and reduced the modality gap more effectively.
rows.check: SONAR's cross-modal similarity exceeds the other similarity types. The alignment was trained for, so it is induced; no version.

rows.subject: SALMONN-7B
rows.operation_detail: Correlated the proportion of shared tokens in parallel sentences with pairwise representation similarity after the word-embedding layer.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between shared-token proportion and pairwise similarity.
rows.baseline: No correlation; reported p-value is the significance reference.
rows.note: Authors report a positive correlation and relate it to fragmented tokenization; they note it may be stronger after disentangling resource-level effects.
rows.check: Correlation r=0.228 (p=1.48e-06) between shared tokens and similarity at SALMONN's embedding layer. This is a tokenizer artifact in within-model cross-lingual similarity, not metric or data dependence of cross-model convergence.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Language resource groups and token-sharing differences in the tested speech-text representations
reader_labels.reason: Similarity differs by resource level (r4–r6), and SALMONN's pairwise similarity is positively correlated with shared-token proportion (r21).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Seamless and SALMONN cross-modal and cross-lingual comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Alignment rises across layers but has early dips, low-resource limitations, and modality gaps that can remain larger than language gaps (r1–r10, r12–r13, r18–r19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SONAR, explicitly trained to align modality and language representations
reader_labels.reason: SONAR's pooling and alignment training reduce the modality gap more effectively, and cross-modal similarity exceeds other similarity types for most languages (r11, r20).
